title: Microaggressions: Recognizing Messages and Responding with Care
before: How everyday comments can signal exclusion or lowered credibility based on identity, and how to respond with care and proportion.

turns.text: Microaggressions: Recognizing Messages and Responding with Care is about the everyday comments and habits that can communicate exclusion or diminished credibility based on identity. The course helps DSD staff recognize those messages, respond with care, and notice how repeated interactions can shape service and workplace opportunity over time, even when each moment looks small on its own.

It begins with a sentence that sounds like praise: “You are surprisingly knowledgeable.” The surprise carries a message, because it suggests the speaker expected less. The course asks you to separate the part that describes the contribution from the part that compares the person with an unstated expectation, and to consider context before deciding what the comment communicates.

The definition is careful in a way I appreciate. A microaggression is an everyday verbal, behavioral, or environmental message that can communicate identity-based exclusion or diminished standing. “Micro” describes the everyday scale, not a guaranteed small effect. And not every discourtesy is identity-based, so the course asks you to explain the connection rather than rushing to a label.

The first service example is one that can happen with the best intentions. An adult asks about a service option, and staff answer the accompanying support person instead, never returning to the adult. The adult then asks to be addressed directly. You will choose the most useful next response, and the explanations show how each option affects both the adult and the support person.

Intent and impact come up throughout the course, and they answer different questions. Intent concerns what the speaker meant, while impact concerns what the exchange did or communicated. A good intention does not erase a reported effect, and a reported effect does not reveal every motive. The course suggests acknowledging the specific action before defending your intention, which is harder than it sounds in the moment.

Repetition matters too, because one question about someone’s background may be welcome, but repeatedly rejecting their answer can communicate that it does not count. The listener may notice one exchange while the person receiving it recognizes a pattern. The course also reminds us not to make the affected person explain an identity, confront anyone, or accept an apology.

The workplace case brings this together when a new employee identifies a missing service address, and a colleague comments on their “unexpectedly good English.” The discussion moves on, and the address question disappears. You will decide what response best preserves the contribution. The course also offers a short exercise on turning “surprisingly articulate” into specific feedback about the work itself.

In a listening session example, staff ask the only participant from one community to explain what “their people” need. That request turns participation into a burden of representation and can leave other experiences unheard. You will practice a more respectful invitation, and the course explains how images, examples, and introductions can send similar environmental messages.

The course is clear about roles: a learning conversation can offer support, but it does not decide whether conduct meets a legal or workplace standard. Staff use current agency reporting routes and the responsibilities of their actual role, and an apology, a course result, or a consultant conversation should never become a gate to an applicable process.

And it treats repair as more than a sentence. If credit, wording, or an opportunity was affected, the course asks what correction is appropriate, and it notes that repair is more credible when behavior changes. It also looks past the single comment to the routine that carries it, like an introduction habit or a speaking rule, because changing the routine can matter even without knowing anyone’s full motive.

As you begin, think of an everyday exchange you have witnessed or been part of where a comment landed differently than intended. What was said, and what might it have communicated? You can keep that reflection entirely private. The course will help you name the action, consider its effect, and choose a response that fits your role.

guidance.title: Why the term needs care
guidance.text: The word microaggression gives us a way to notice messages that are easy to dismiss one at a time. It names an everyday scale, not a small effect, because the same kind of message can build up across many interactions. At the same time, not every rude moment is about identity. Explaining the connection you see is more useful than reaching for the label quickly.

guidance.title: A response that fits
guidance.text: Look back at the response you rewrote. In your own role, which kind of response would usually fit best: a brief interruption, a private check-in, or an appropriate formal route? What would you need to know about the affected person’s wishes first? Consider, too, what would still remain unknown after you responded, and how you might notice whether the recurring routine changed.
